newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST-Sharp drop seen for FCL Paper.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Sharp drop seen for FCL Paper.

text.p: Sharp cyclical downturns in pulp and paper are likely to make for grim reading when Fletcher Paper reports its first half result next week, analysts said on Thursday.
They said FCL Paper would be lucky to break even and that a loss was more likely, against a NZ$186 million profit for the six months to December, 1995.

Hopes late last year of a cyclical upturn have failed to materialise, and the industry still faces additional problems of overcapacity and excess inventory and a mature market for its key product, newsprint.

David Stanley at Doyle Paterson Brown expects a loss of around NZ$30 million before abnormals but a smaller loss after abnormals. FCL Paper stood to make an abnormal gain of about NZ$30 million from the government's payment to Tasman Pulp and Paper to exit its commitment under the Tasman log contracts.
This would partly offset provisions for FCL Canada's business restructuring of around NZ$8.0 million, leaving a net abnormal gain of around $20-25 million.
Pulp and fine paper prices had fallen sharply, picked up a little, then drifted off again over the period.
Newsprint had suffered a sustained fall since peaking a year ago and has been on a slow slide ever since, but prices were expected to improve over the coming quarter.
"All of that has impacted negatively on the result," Stanley said. Among the few bright spots, FCL Canada's solid wood products operation was expected to have performed well.
But there appeared little immediate likelihood of a solution to worldwide overcapacity and excess inventory.
"As the world grows faster than capacity increases, then things should start to improve," Stanley said.
Over the last two years capacity had grown, demand had risen, then swung down savagely. What followed was excess inventory build-up then de-stocking.
"It sent a lot of confusing signals to the pulp and paper industry, so it's taken a while for that to be digested. A somewhat unpalatable experience," he said.
Newsprint in the West seen as a mature market, with only minimal growth in U.S. consumption. European consumption had been in line with GDP growth.
That left the prospect of growth in the emerging economies, where there had also been new capacity coming on stream.
John Cairns at Cavill White Securities said there was every indication pulp prices were weakening again, with no let up in inventories.
If there were to be an improvement at all in prices, Cairns expected that to occur in the latter part of this year.
"So in terms of the earnings outlook for the full year it will probably book a loss, but we would expect them to maintain the dividend," he said.
"The market is focusing on the stage in the rate of recovery in prices, which is anyone's guess. Everyone has called it wrong in terms of the rate of recovery," he said.

The industry world-wide was undergoing change, he said, as evidenced by the recent merger of Abitibi-Price and Stone-Consolidated Corp, creating the world's largest newsprint producer by a wide margin.
Cairns said that represented an attempt by the major players to reduce costs and, more importantly, concentrate on getting more leverage out of consumers.
-- Wellington Newsroom (64-4-4734746).
